accuracy.evidence: Checked against the English national curriculum Appendix 2 (DfE 2013) Year 5 statements: degrees of possibility using adverbs (perhaps, surely) or modal verbs (might, should, will, must); relative clauses beginning with who, which, where, when, whose, that or an omitted relative pronoun; brackets, dashes or commas to indicate parenthesis; commas to clarify meaning or avoid ambiguity; and the Year 5 terminology list. Modal meanings of ability, permission and obligation follow the Cambridge Grammar of English.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the real Year 5 slips: calling maybe or perhaps a modal verb (the spot step uses Maybe as a trap tile and the challenge offers maybe and always), not knowing can is a modal (prediction), treating should as strong as must (prediction), using which for people (relative clause feedback), writing should of (mastery m3), leaving off the closing comma of a parenthesis (practice p4) and thinking parenthesis only means brackets (the step mixes commas, dashes and brackets).

lab_distinct.evidence: The flagmodal lab is built around certainty: modal chips dropped onto a possible, likely and certain scale, a five-sector certainty dial matched to a rain forecast percentage, word tiles where the modal must be found among main verbs and an adverb of possibility, a relative pronoun dragged into a dashed gap, and chunks lifted out to test for parenthesis. No other flag lab uses a gauge or a lift-out test and the 30% shingle gate passed.

lab_teaches.evidence: Steps go from meaning to form: first the certainty order of the modals, then using that order against evidence, then finding the modal as a helper before the main verb, then the relative clause and its pronouns, then parenthesis with the lift-out test. Each done message states the rule, for example 'Weak evidence needs a weak modal', and the wrong-answer messages explain why, such as 'Leave is the main verb. The modal verb comes just before it.'

predictions.evidence: Three predictions come before evidence with tempting wrong answers: whether should is as sure as must (many children say yes, then the scale places them in different boxes), whether can is a modal verb (often thought to be a main verb, then a tile proves it), and whether a sentence still works once a parenthesis is lifted out (some expect it to break, then the Without it line shows the sentence).

challenge_feedback.evidence: The Challenge cycles five questions on certainty, modal versus adverb, whose versus who and which, picking the parenthesis and ambiguity. Each wrong option has a tag (weak, adverb, who, which, core, noverb, short) with its own explanation; picking 'It has no verb' for the telescope sentence explains that saw is the verb and the problem is who holds the telescope. Button order rotates.

readability.evidence: Kid text reads at FK 2.4 with short sentences and one worked example per idea, such as 'It should rain means it is likely', inside the family limit of 5.0 for a 9 to 10 year old. Adult text reads at FK 7.9, under 10.0, and keeps every statutory term: modal verb, relative pronoun, relative clause, parenthesis, bracket, dash, cohesion and ambiguity. Lab prompts are one or two sentences.

no_filler.evidence: Each kid paragraph teaches one term with an example sentence. The adult text gives the statutory content, the terms and grammar rules for modals, the common mistakes with a fix (lift the part out and read what is left) and a step by step account of the lab. The family tip uses a real weather forecast to practise modals and parenthesis together.

mobile.evidence: Walked on iPhone 13 and a 360 by 740 viewport in light and dark themes: word tiles wrap into centred lines, chips and zone boxes are at least 50 pixels tall, the dial responds to a drag anywhere on the gauge and also has Less sure, More sure and Lock in buttons, and every canvas drag has a matching button so nothing needs fine motor control.

accessibility.evidence: axe ran clean in both themes on desktop and phone. The canvas aria-label tracks the current sentence, status text goes to a polite live region, every button has a text label, gap fills are read out as words, and colour is never the only signal: correct answers also get a tick and a sentence, wrong ones get an explanation.
